scenes.tts: By the 1950s the lock-and-key picture decorated every textbook — and Daniel Koshland knew it was incomplete, because of water.
scenes.visual: 1950s; lock-and-key in every textbook; Koshland knew it incomplete; water
scenes.narration: By the 1950s the lock-and-key picture decorated every textbook — and Daniel Koshland knew it was incomplete, because of water.

scenes.tts: If an active site sat permanently open and waiting, water molecules, smaller than any substrate, should slip in constantly and trigger chaos. They don't.
scenes.visual: permanently open site; water slips in, chaos; they don't
scenes.narration: If an active site sat permanently open and waiting, water molecules, smaller than any substrate, should slip in constantly and trigger chaos. They don't.

scenes.tts: So something must change when the real substrate arrives: the hand doesn't just slide into a pre-formed glove; the glove changes shape around the hand. Binding induces a conformational change — "induced fit" — and water is too small to force it.
scenes.visual: substrate arrives; glove changes shape around hand; induced fit; water too small

scenes.tts: The idea cut so hard against the dogma that standard journals blocked it (one reviewer's verdict became famous); Koshland slipped it into PNAS in 1958 through a loophole.
scenes.visual: journals block the idea; reviewer verdict; PNAS 1958 loophole

scenes.tts: X-ray crystallography later proved him right: enzymes flex, shift, and clamp down. He had moved biochemistry from a science of static structures to one of moving machines.
